24.46: 24.46 Yet doctrine. RABANUS. The writer of this work signifies that the book is mystical, and useful to read. For historically it teaches morality, and allegorically the sacrament of the faith.
24.47: 24.47 See, etc. The ecclesiastical teacher profits not only himself, but also others by writing and teaching: whence, They that are learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and they that instruct many to justice, as stars for all eternity, Daniel 12.
25.2: 25.2 A man and a woman. RABANUS. Whence Paul, Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church, Ephesians 5. We can take the spirit in the man, the soul in the woman, who if they agree in the fear and love of God, whatever they ask shall be done to them, whence: If two of you shall agree, it shall be done to them, Matthew 18.
25.3: 25.3 Three kinds. THE SAME. These can be transferred to the devil, etc., down to because he would not be subject to his Creator.
25.5: 25.5 Those things which in youth. He who in youth learns not wisdom, in old age has not its fruit. Whence, A slack hand has wrought poverty, but the hand of the strong prepares riches, Proverbs 10. But he who meditates in the law of the Lord will give his fruit in due season, Psalm 1.
25.6: 25.6 How beautiful. THE SAME. A hoary head becomes, etc., down to it is not lawful for them to be ignorant of the knowledge and wisdom of the law.
25.9: 25.9 Nine things not to be suspected, etc. With the heart we believe unto justice, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation, Romans 10. There are therefore nine things not to be suspected, that is alien from every suspicion of falsity, which right faith begets in man.
25.13: 25.13 Wisdom. Which is to shun evil. Whence, And behold the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to depart from evil is understanding, Job 28. Hence it is that one is added over to the kinds of virtues.
25.16: 25.16 The fear of God. RABANUS. Because as the number nine is imperfect, etc., down to but let not the presence of God, which you embrace, and desire to enjoy forever, forsake you.
25.17: 25.17 Every wound. There is no greater grace than true joy of mind, nor greater wound than the sadness of a deceitful heart in idolatry or in heresy, because in its wickedness is all malice.
25.18: 25.18 And every wound. He sees the wound of the heart who understands the injury of his perversity, but he does not see who by penance does not correct.
25.22: 25.22 There is no head, etc. RABANUS. The wickedness of heretics compared, etc., down to therefore her cohabitation is harmful to all.
25.26: 25.26 All malice is short. All malice is small in comparison with idolatry and heretical perversity, because they sin not through the frailty of the flesh, but through pride of mind.
25.30: 25.30 If a woman have the principality. Historically he shows how harmful the principality of a woman is, etc., down to she will be contrary to the husband, that is to the Catholic teacher, by thinking perverse things and teaching wicked.
26.1: 26.1 Of a good woman. RABANUS. As before he blamed the wicked woman, etc., down to and in the future will rejoice in the receiving of rewards.
26.4: 26.4 Of a rich man. The rich or the poor coming to the grace of Christ with devout mind will forever enjoy the pleasantness of the vision of God, because God is not a respecter of persons.
26.5: 26.5 Of three. By these similitudes he calls those who are separated from the unity of true religion, that is Jews, pagans, heretics, and false Christians.
26.6: 26.6 The accusation of a city. The folly of fools. For as brute animals know not how to discern between friend and enemy, and between good and evil; so the foolish know not the distance between Catholic and heretical doctrine, but obey true and false teachers alike. Against whom it is said elsewhere, Immediately he follows her as an ox led to the victim, and as a lamb wantonly, and knows not that he is drawn to the slaughter, Proverbs 7. But the cunning of heretics deceives the unwary not with an open face but deceitfully.
26.11: 26.11 A drunken woman. He describes the habit of a harlot, who by motion of the body and motion of the eyes displays lust. Mystically, however, it signifies the heretic, who in pride of sense and eloquence of words boasts his fornication, that he may more easily attract lovers of novelties itching in the ears, who turn away their hearing from the truth and are turned to fables.
26.12: 26.12 The fornication of a woman. RABANUS. By these three he shows the curiosity of the human mind, etc., down to by the pride of life, when he added, You shall be as gods, Genesis 3.
26.16: 26.16 Shall make fat his bones. With charity, namely, whence: He that keeps my commandments, he it is that loves me, and shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him, John 14.
26.18: 26.18 A woman, etc. Because the wisdom of God imbues the souls of the elect, and grants them guard of the mouth and efficacy of work, nor permits them to turn from her, because everyone that is born of God sins not, namely by violating faith or charity: Because the seed of God, that is the word by which he was reborn, he has in himself.
26.23: 26.23 Golden pillars. Teachers shining with wisdom are set upon silver bases, when in holy Scripture they are distinguished by their preaching.
26.25: 26.25 In two. RABANUS. Wisdom marks, etc., down to or, the path of truth forsaken, follows the byways of error.
26.28: 26.28 Hardly is he cleared. RABANUS. The worst act, not an honest thing, is condemned. That merchant is to be abominated who through immoderate ambition burdens his wares more with perjury than with price.
27.1: 27.1 For poverty, etc., RABANUS. As in the midst. Here by comparison, etc., down to and in the future eternal punishment remains.
27.5: 27.5 As in the shaking of a sieve. THE SAME. As a sieve, etc., down to: Satan has desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat.
27.7: 27.7 As the dressing of wood. THE SAME. Every tree, etc., down to the cultivation of wood therefore in its fruit manifests its quality.
27.8: 27.8 Before speech. Because speech shows thought. As if to say: Let no one praise him whom he has not known by manifest signs worthy of praise. Speech, however, can be taken for good work, that we praise no one before proof of good works. Whence: Praise not any man before his death.
27.13: 27.13 In the midst. RABANUS. He teaches temperance and caution in speaking, etc., down to: But he that shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven, Matthew 5.
27.15: 27.15 Speech, etc. Because as their action is contrary to the good, so speech is prone to speaking evils, heavy to hearing.
27.17: 27.17 He that discloses. He shows in what friendship is chiefly injured, in the evil, namely, of betrayal, which loses faith, and does not keep the equity of friendship, and therefore dissipates charity.
27.22: 27.22 As a roe. The roe, a wild goat, so called as if taking steep places. The roes are called ibexes or birds, because like birds they hold high and lofty places: and dwell in heights, so that from their height they are scarcely visible to human eyes. These if ever they perceive the adversity of wild beasts or men: casting themselves from the high peaks, receive themselves unhurt on their horns in the branches of trees.
27.24: 27.24 To uncover, etc. RABANUS. He shows the inconstancy of manners of the betrayer, etc., down to: An apostate man, an unprofitable man, walks with a perverse mouth, winks with the eyes, presses with the foot, etc. Proverbs 6.
27.30: 27.30 He that does a most wicked counsel. Because he sees not that his day will come. For the heretic or schismatic thinks his sect better than Catholic truth: whence he deceives himself.
28.8: 28.8 Remember. RABANUS. He who fears God restrains anger or fury, and forgets not the covenant of God, who says: Forgive, and you shall be forgiven, Luke 9.
28.13: 28.13 A contention. Indiscreet action: whence, Be not over just, nor more wise than is necessary, lest you be astonished. Immoderate discipline therefore excites the heat of fury, and a bold speech the shedding of blood.
28.19: 28.19 The third tongue. Heretical doctrine, which agrees neither with the Old nor New Testament, and troubles the hearts of hearers, and going from nation to nation, stirs up sedition.
28.21: 28.21 The stroke, however. Worse is the destruction of the soul which heretics kill, than any torment of the body. Blessed is he that is covered. Blessed is he who consents not to heretics, and whose heart their eloquence does not subvert, because as he is alien from their malice, so he is separated from their punishment.
28.28: 28.28 Hedge in your ears. After he has rooted out the evil of the tongue, he turns to the doctrine of the hearer.
29.5: 29.5 Till they receive. RABANUS. The fear of God better cures such a disease. For he who fears God as ever present, intends to defraud no one.
29.10: 29.10 For many, etc. THE SAME. He marks those who wish to harm no one, but for fear of perishable things will not benefit. Against whom it is said: Lay not up to yourselves treasures on earth, Matthew 6.
29.12: 29.12 For the commandment's sake. Mercy is to be shown to all the needy, nor is charity of neighbor to be lost for avarice.
29.13: 29.13 And hide not. For he who sees his brother in need, and shuts up his bowels from him, how does the charity of God abide in him?
29.16: 29.16 Above the shield of the mighty, etc. Alms avails more against the darts of the enemy than earthly arms: because these beget doubtful victory, that most certain, that death may be swallowed up in victory.
29.20: 29.20 The grace of a surety, etc. The teacher, namely, who for faith and good works promises eternal life. This sentence reproves Pelagius who puts free will before grace, whereas the elect are freed by grace alone.
29.23: 29.23 He that has lost, etc. That is, he who keeps not the unity of faith and sincerity of the law, but is entangled in various errors.
29.27: 29.27 Recover your neighbor. He counsels that according to your means you afford comfort to your neighbor, and so provide for yourself that you fall not into the snare.
29.28: 29.28 The chief thing for life, etc. RABANUS. He teaches frugality, and hospitality and honesty, etc., down to and the Lord made coats of skins for the first parents after sin.
29.29: 29.29 Better is the life of a poor man, etc. Literally. It is better to take a slender living under a mean cottage in security, than to seek splendid feasts with weariness in uncertain places. THE SAME. Allegorically. Better is the life, etc., down to where is labor and superfluous care.
29.30: 29.30 Least. THE SAME. Let what you have suffice you, etc., down to a good name is better than many delights.
29.33: 29.33 Pass on. As: You who delight in another's hospitality, return to your own, and feed yourself and others by your labor. Seek not superfluous food from another's house. The reception of neighbors suffices you.
29.34: 29.34 The reproach. RABANUS. Mystically, however, the ecclesiastical man is admonished, etc., down to but in the future examination let him bear the eternal reproach of confusion.
30.1: 30.1 He that loves his son. RABANUS. He admonishes fathers both carnal and spiritual to instruct their sons diligently, that they live honestly, lest by wantonness they run about after the teachings of others.
30.8: 30.8 An unbroken horse. An unbroken horse goes to the precipice; an undisciplined son rushes into sin. He teaches therefore spiritual fathers to instruct and correct their sons; not to loosen the reins immoderately, lest they fall into the baseness of vices, and themselves bear everlasting disgrace.
